newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain inflation loses sting after February CPI.
newsitem.headline: Spain inflation loses sting after February CPI.

text.p: Spanish inflation, a key hindrance to Spain's becoming part of the European single currency in 1999, looks tamed after a sharp fall in February consumer price data, analysts said on Thursday.
"In just two months, we have come down seven tenths which is a push for Spanish convergence in the European monetary union and market credibility," said Spain's Economy Secretary Cristobal Montoro.

Given the lower-than-expected consumer price index (CPI), which fell 0.1 percent from January and pushed down the yearly rise to 2.5 percent from 2.9 percent a month ago, analysts are now revising down their initial forecasts for the full 1997 year.

It is also helping prepare the ground for Spain to meet inflation requirements for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) and increasing the probability it will undershoot the government's goal to end the year at a rate of 2.6 percent.

"Harmonised CPI could be 0.1 percent lower than the domestic index so, the Spanish (1997) average could be around 2.2 percent, which allows Spain to meet Maastricht's criteria," said Felix Gonzalez, analyst at Beta Capital in Madrid.
In terms of January's harmonised index, Spain and Portugal stand at 2.8 percent, a tenth above the European threshold for the month of 2.7 percent.
"We expect (domestic) inflation to fall around 2.0 percent in May, or even lower, with an average rate around 2.3 percent versus the 2.5 percent we expected before," said Gonzalez.
A drop in olive oil, which falls into the processed food category, and stable performances in other components helped keep February CPI subdued.
"Olive oil, as it was the case in January, had a very big positive impact," said one analyst who declined to be named. She also said the fall in electrical tariffs helped keep inflation tame.
February core inflation, excluding volatile fresh food and energy prices, rose 0.1 percent from January and 2.3 percent year-on-year.

"Core inflation showed a very good performance, with each component in a bit lower than expected. This is prompting us to make our forecast more positive for the year. We expect that the average in the year will not be higher than 2.4 percent," said Antoni Espasa, economist at University Carlos III, who expects headline CPI to fall to about 2.0 percent in May before picking up again toward 2.4 or 2.5 percent by the end of the year.
Analysts added that the truckers strike in February failed to have the negative impact some had feared it might.
The only worrying issue was seen coming from service inflation, which rose 0.4 percent from January to 3.4 percent year-on-year.
"This issue is the one worrying the most the Bank of Spain, as they said, and still its seems to be very stubborn," said Colin Warren at Tokai Bank in London.
